The Chevron Era
Although Chevron quickly became one of the most highly cited 
Supreme Court cases in all of American law, some of the Court’s 
subsequent cases did not give the opinion an expansive reading. Those later 
Supreme Court cases curtailed the doctrine’s domain; other cases, however, 
took some of the broad language in Chevron to its logical consequences. 
Three aspects of the post-Chevron cases are worth highlighting
First: A prominent example of a case limiting Chevron's domain was 
United States v. Mead Corp,, 533 U.S. 218 (2001), decided approximately a 
decade and a half after Chevron itself. Mead qualified Chevron by holding 
that the measure of deference that a court gave to an agency intArpreta tinn 
depended in part on the elaborateness of the agency’s procedures. Under 
Mead, interpretations announced in notice-and-comment rules and formal 
adjudications presumptively received Chevron deference, whereas 
interpretations in informal adjudications received Chevron deference only 
if other factors were met. Writing for the Court, Justice Souter reasoned 
that “[t]he fair measure of deference to an agency administAring its own 
statute has been understood to vary with circumstances, and courts have 
looked to the degree of the agency’s care, its consistency, formahty, and 
relative expertness, and to the persuasiveness of the agency’s position.” 
Mead explained that this approach ‘Tias produced a spectrum of judicial 
responses, from great respect at one end, to near indifference at the other,” 
with the Court “tailoring] deference to variety” and conferring Chevron 
deference based on “a variety of indicators.” Mead held that the agency’s 
interpretation was not eligible for Chevron deference, but rather “respect 
according to its persuasiveness” under Skidmore.
Mead's approach thus appeared to eschew the simplicity of a two-step 
process. Some called the initial question that Mead added to the Chevron 
analysis ''Chevron Step Zero.” In his dissent. Justice Scalia characterized 
Mead as “an avulsive change” and claimed that “[w]hat was previously a 
general presumption of authority in agencies to resolve ambiguity in the 
statutes they have been authorized to enforce has been changed to a 
presumption of no such authority.” And he criticized the majority’s 
‘iDreathing new life into the anachronism of Skidmore," describing the “rule 
of Skidmore deference [as] an empty truism and a trifling statement of the 
obvious: A judge should take into account the well-considered views of 
expert observers.”
